slots.practicalActivity: Generate a synthetic 50,000-row customer table, save it both as CSV and as Parquet, and compare the file sizes (the lesson's own run found Parquet at about 31% of the CSV size). Read back only 3 columns with pd.read_parquet(path, columns=[...]), then run a stratified 70/15/15 train/validation/test split with random_state=42 and confirm the churn rate stays identical across all 3 splits.
slots.deliverable: Printed CSV vs. Parquet byte sizes with the percentage saved, a 3-column selective Parquet read, and a 3-way split showing matching churn rates in train, validation, and test.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's tenure_bucket (0-12/13-36/37-72 months) and spend_per_ticket features in pandas on your 50,000-row table, then compute churn rate by tenure bucket and confirm it falls as tenure rises, matching the lesson's pattern (roughly 27.5%, 21.8%, 14.1%). Write (do not execute) the awswrangler wr.s3.to_parquet(..., dataset=True, database="churn_db", table="customers") call that would register this feature table in the Glue Data Catalog.
slots.deliverable: A churn-rate-by-tenure-bucket table from your own feature engineering, plus the catalog-registration code snippet documenting how it would be shared across Athena, Redshift, and SageMaker.

slots.practicalActivity: Load your customer table into a local SQLite database as an Athena stand-in, and run the lesson's 3 SQL patterns: a GROUP BY plan churn-rate query, a reproducible WHERE customer_id % 10 = 0 sample (not Athena's random TABLESAMPLE), and a CTAS-style query that buckets customers into new/mid/loyal tenure bands with a CASE expression. Confirm the tenure-band churn rates match the pandas numbers from the previous lesson.
slots.deliverable: 3 executed SQL queries against the local SQLite stand-in with their result sets, and a confirmation note that the SQL tenure-band churn rates match the earlier pandas feature-engineering results.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the point-in-time feature query in SQLite (orders counted and summed only before a 2024-01-01 cutoff, inside the JOIN condition, not a WHERE clause), train a logistic regression and confirm a realistic test AUC around 0.775. Then deliberately add a feature that includes 2024 orders and watch the AUC jump to a suspicious 1.000, proving the leakage detector. Finally, write 2 scoped IAM JSON policy statements (read-only on raw/, read-write on processed/ and models/) and test them with simple wildcard string matching against 4 sample S3 object keys to confirm which keys each statement would and would not allow.
slots.deliverable: The leakage-safe feature query with its real AUC (around 0.775), the leaky version's inflated AUC (1.000), and 2 IAM policy JSON statements with a wildcard-match test table showing which of 4 sample keys each one allows.

slots.practicalActivity: Without any AWS account, build a boto3 sagemaker client object locally and inspect its service model (client.meta.service_model.operation_model("CreateSpace").input_shape.members, and the same for ListDomains and CreateApp) to confirm the exact parameter names the lesson describes (DomainId, SpaceName, AppType, ResourceSpec). Then work out, on paper, what sagemaker.Session().default_bucket() would name for a placeholder account id and region, and why that name would already satisfy the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess bucket-name rule from the next IAM lesson.
slots.deliverable: Printed parameter lists for the CreateSpace, ListDomains, and CreateApp operations read straight from boto3's service model, plus a written default-bucket name you worked out for a placeholder account/region.

slots.practicalActivity: Run df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() on your 50,000-row customer table and record the real figure, then convert the low-cardinality region and plan columns to pandas category dtype and remeasure, confirming the large drop the lesson found (about 8.1 MB down to about 2.1 MB). Extrapolate your own per-row figure to estimate the memory footprint of a 20-million-row version of the same table, and use that estimate to decide what SageMaker instance size you would actually need.
slots.deliverable: Before/after memory_usage figures for the category-dtype conversion, plus a written extrapolation and instance-size recommendation for a 20-million-row version of the table.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's deliberately messy 20,000-row table (5% missing monthly_spend, 400 duplicated rows, and a leaky exit_survey_sent column recorded after the churn decision), then write a pandas quality-report analogue reporting missing %, duplicate count, and outlier count, plus a single-feature-AUC leakage screen across every numeric column. Clean the data (drop duplicates, impute missing spend, drop the leaky column, one-hot encode), and confirm test AUC drops from the leakage-inflated figure to the honest one once the leaky column is removed.
slots.deliverable: A printed quality report (missing %, duplicates, outliers), a single-feature-AUC ranking that flags the leaky column, and the before/after test AUC (with and without the leaky column) proving which number is trustworthy.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the full script-mode train.py that reads hyperparameters as command-line arguments and reads SM_MODEL_DIR / SM_CHANNEL_TRAIN / SM_CHANNEL_VALIDATION from the environment, run it locally by setting those 3 environment variables yourself, and confirm it prints a validation:accuracy=...; log line and saves model.joblib. Then reformat the same table into the built-in-algorithm CSV convention (label as the first column, no header row), and write a bring-your-own container program that reads hyperparameters.json and a CSV from the documented /opt/ml folder layout, trains, and writes a failure file with a non-zero exit code when a required input file is missing.
slots.deliverable: A script-mode train.py run showing the printed validation:accuracy line and a saved model.joblib, the reformatted label-first/no-header CSV, and 2 runs of the bring-your-own container program (one clean exit 0, one deliberately broken exit 1 with a captured failure-file traceback).

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's local tuning-job stand-in: launch train.py as a subprocess 8 times with randomly sampled n-estimators and max-depth values, pull each run's validation:accuracy out of the log with the documented regular expression, and report the best-scoring candidate. Note which hyperparameter region (shallow trees with many estimators, or deep trees with few) performed best on this noisy data, and explain why that matches what a real SageMaker tuning job's objective-metric regex is for.
slots.deliverable: A table of all 8 candidate hyperparameter combinations with their extracted validation:accuracy, and the single best (n-estimators, max-depth) pair with a one-sentence explanation of the pattern you found.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's 6-run MLflow sweep of random-forest variants (random n_estimators and max_depth choices) against a local tracking URI, logging params, a data_version tag, the fitted model artifact, and val_accuracy for each run, then sort all 6 with mlflow.search_runs(order_by=["metrics.val_accuracy DESC"]). Identify which 2 of your 6 runs happened to draw identical settings and therefore produced identical scores, confirming wasted compute is visible once you track runs.
slots.deliverable: A sorted 6-row MLflow search_runs table (run name, n_estimators, max_depth, val_accuracy), with the 2 duplicate-setting runs identified and flagged as wasted compute.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the 3 local scripts from the lesson's pipeline sketch: a preprocessing script (dropna, drop_duplicates, 75/25 split into train/validation folders), a training script (fits a model, prints validation:accuracy), and an evaluation script (writes a JSON accuracy report). Chain them in a small Python runner that mimics a processing-then-training-then-evaluate-then-condition pipeline, and run the whole chain twice with a condition threshold of 0.6 (should register the model) and then 0.8 (should fail the gate), confirming the same code and data produce 2 different outcomes purely from the parameter change.
slots.deliverable: Console output from both pipeline runs: one showing "-> RegisterModel" at threshold 0.6 and one showing "-> Fail" at threshold 0.8, with the evaluation.json report from each run.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a small orders_30d-over-time table for 2 customers across 3 months, and write the online_store() function (keeps only the latest event_time per customer_id) and confirm its output against the full history. Add a late-arriving record with an earlier event_time for customer 1 and confirm the offline history keeps it while the online view still shows only the true latest record. Then use pandas.merge_asof to build a point-in-time-correct training set, confirming a label dated mid-February correctly receives the February feature snapshot rather than a later one.
slots.deliverable: The online-store view (latest record per customer) and the full offline history after the late-arriving record, plus the merge_asof training table proving each label row received the feature value that was true as of its own label date.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the 4 SageMaker inference handler functions (model_fn, input_fn, predict_fn, output_fn) for the churn model, supporting both application/json and text/csv content types, and chain them in a local harness exactly the way the model server would. Test it with a JSON request, a 3-row CSV request, and a request with an unsupported content type, confirming you reproduce probabilities close to the lesson's own run (0.4114 and 0.3291) and a clear rejection for the bad request.
slots.deliverable: Printed output for all 3 test requests (JSON, CSV, and the rejected bad-content-type request) from your own chained handler harness, matching the expected churn probabilities.

slots.practicalActivity: Reuse your lesson-15 inference handlers to simulate a batch-transform job: split 500 validation customers into mini-batches of 200 CSV lines, call the handlers on each mini-batch the way the transform driver would, and confirm you get exactly 3 run() calls and a joined 500-row output file with predictions in the same order as the input. Then sketch the ServerlessConfig settings (MemorySizeInMB, MaxConcurrency) you would choose for an internal demo tool used only a few times a day.
slots.deliverable: The simulated batch job's 500-row joined output with the 3-mini-batch-call confirmation, plus a short written choice of serverless memory size and concurrency with a one-sentence justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Use botocore's Stubber to validate, offline and with no AWS account, the exact request shapes for create_model_package_group, create_model_package, and update_model_package. Then write the lesson's local approval-gate rule in plain Python (validation AUC >= 0.75 and better than the currently approved version) and apply it to 3 candidate models (2 logistic-regression settings and a gradient-boosting model), assigning each one Approved, Rejected, or Superseded based on the rule.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation that all 3 boto3 calls passed offline parameter validation, plus a 3-row decision table (model, validation AUC, assigned status) produced by your own approval-gate function.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the PSI/KS drift check and apply it to 3 simulated production weeks: a normal week, a week where inputs shift sharply but AUC barely moves, and a week where inputs look normal yet AUC collapses toward random, confirming why input-drift monitoring alone would have missed the third failure. Then build the cost-scenario table comparing a real-time endpoint running 24x7 for 30 days, the same endpoint deleted after a 2-day test, and a 15-minutes-per-night batch job, at a placeholder $0.20/instance-hour rate, and verify the managed-spot-training savings formula with the lesson's 100-of-500-billable-seconds example (80.0% saved).
slots.deliverable: A 3-week drift-vs-AUC table showing the drift-without-harm week and the harm-without-drift-flag week, plus the 3-scenario cost table and the confirmed 80.0% spot-training savings calculation.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Train, Deploy and Monitor a Model on AWS

slots.practicalActivity: Generate the capstone's seeded 6,000-row Riverbend Meals churn table, confirm the 38.1% churn rate, split 60/20/20, and train both the dummy baseline (AUC 0.5, zero recall) and the first scikit-learn pipeline, confirming you clear the kickoff's AUC >= 0.75 criterion. Compute recall by subscription plan and find the weak segment the lesson's own run found on weekly-plan customers, then set up the churn-capstone/ repository layout exactly as specified.
slots.deliverable: Baseline-vs-first-model AUC and recall figures confirming the AUC criterion is met, a recall-by-plan table exposing the weak segment, and the created repository folder structure.

slots.practicalActivity: Run train.py in script mode locally, reading its SM_* environment variables, and confirm it prints validation:auc and validation:recall. Package model.tar.gz with model.joblib and a code/inference.py folder, and test all 4 inference handler functions with a CSV request, a JSON request, and a request with an unsupported content type. Then apply the capstone's monitoring decision rule (quality below the AUC gate -> retrain, drift with acceptable quality -> investigate, otherwise OK) to its 3 simulated weeks of traffic and confirm your verdicts match OK / INVESTIGATE / RETRAIN.
slots.deliverable: The script-mode training output, a built and inspected model.tar.gz, handler test output for all 3 request types, and a 3-week monitoring verdict table matching OK / INVESTIGATE / RETRAIN.

slots.practicalActivity: Review your capstone against all 6 kickoff criteria with concrete evidence for each one. Choose a per-plan decision threshold on the validation set by maximizing F1, apply it exactly once to the untouched test set, and confirm overall recall rises while precision falls, the same trade-off the lesson's own run found (recall 0.556 to 0.726, precision 0.708 to 0.609). Write a model card (purpose, data, metrics, limits, do-not-use-for, monitoring) and complete the 5-step AWS cleanup checklist.
slots.deliverable: A criteria-by-criteria review with evidence, a before/after per-plan-threshold precision/recall comparison, a written model card, and a completed cleanup checklist.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can run the full data-science workflow on AWS — S3, Glue, Athena, and Redshift for data; SageMaker for training, tuning, pipelines, and the feature store; real-time and batch inference; and drift, cost, and governance monitoring — and has shipped a deployed, monitored churn model as a portfolio piece, working in either AWS or Azure as the job requires.
